## Discussion

By systematically re-mining public human RNA-seq, recovering the non-human reads that standard transcriptomic pipelines discard, we resolved the productive status of cutaneous HPV across the spectrum from healthy skin to carcinoma, while controlling for the two confounders that have dogged this question: laboratory contamination and sequencing depth. Three findings stand out. First, HPV signal in archived RNA-seq is dominated by cell-line and engineered material and by the integrated mucosal types HPV16/HPV18, so that genuine primary skin carries HPV at only 2–4%. Second, and centrally, HPV in cutaneous neoplasia (cSCC/AK) is present only as a transcriptionally inactive trace, not as productive infection, and this gap is not an artefact of how deeply the libraries were sequenced. Third, the same assay readily detects productive infection where it genuinely occurs: in warts and epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV), and in a minority of bona fide primary-skin lesions carrying gamma- and alpha-HPV.

### Trace, not productive: a population-scale transcriptomic test of the hit-and-run model

The defining prediction of the "hit-and-run" hypothesis is that beta-HPV acts early in cutaneous carcinogenesis but is dispensable for tumour maintenance, so that viral load and transcription decline as lesions progress and are minimal or absent in established carcinoma [@howley2015]. The experimental backbone of this model is genetic: in transgenic and infection systems, deleting the viral oncogenes after lesions have formed, or transplanting secondary tumours, leaves carcinoma growth unaffected and viral genomes undetectable [@viarisio2018; @dorfer2021], and in human tissue viral load and transcription are highest in early precursor lesions and fall in established tumours [@borgogna2018]. Our data provide a complementary, population-scale transcriptomic read-out of the same prediction. Across `r comma(stats$neo_n)` cSCC/AK libraries, only `r stats$neo_pos_floor` reached the control-calibrated detection floor (`r pp(stats$neo_pctfloor)`%), against `r pp(stats$ctrl_pctfloor)`% of productive controls, and the tier's median burden was `r formatC(stats$neo_medrpm, format="f", digits=3)` RPM against `r comma(stats$ctrl_medrpm)` RPM in controls. Neoplasia does carry HPV more often than clean skin, both as a trace signal (any read; OR `r fo(stats$m2a_or)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m2a_p)`) and, marginally, at the detection floor (OR `r fo(stats$m2b_or)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m2b_p)`; halved to OR `r fo(stats$m2b_or_cut)` once the `r stats$cin_n` mucosal HPV16 cases are removed). But that elevation is a rise from near-zero to near-zero, and it is not converted into productive burden by any amount of sequencing. This is precisely the residual footprint, rather than active infection, that hit-and-run predicts. It also extends a long-standing but contested single-study observation. More than a decade ago, transcriptome sequencing of cSCC concluded that HPV is "not active" in these tumours [@arron2011]; our results confirm that conclusion at two orders of magnitude greater scale and show that it is not an artefact of shallow sequencing: the neoplasia libraries were sequenced almost four times more deeply than the productive controls (median `r mreads(stats$neo_medreads)` vs `r mreads(stats$ctrl_medreads)` reads), and even the deepest among them, at `r p1(stats$neo_maxreads)`M reads, did not cross the productive threshold.

That said, transcriptomic absence cannot by itself adjudicate the mechanism. A trace, non-productive footprint is equally compatible with hit-and-run oncogenesis and with the alternative, immunosurveillance-based view in which commensal beta-HPV is not an oncogenic driver at all but a marker whose control by antiviral T cells is itself protective against skin cancer [@strickley2019]. Our cross-sectional snapshot of bulk transcription measures viral activity, not causation, and cannot distinguish a virus that has "hit and run" from one that was never causally required. What it does establish, robustly and at scale, is the phenomenology both models must accommodate: established cutaneous neoplasia does not host productive HPV infection.

### Productive cutaneous HPV is real, but it is the property of warts and EV

The trace-level neoplasia result is not a failure of sensitivity. The assay recovered abundant productive infection in the positive-control lesions: `r round(stats$m3_ctrl_pct)`% of targeted wart/EV libraries met the strict L1 major-capsid criterion, spanning the expected cutaneous repertoire (HPV2/27/57, HPV6/11, and diverse beta/gamma types), consistent with the differentiation-coupled late programme that defines productive papillomavirus infection [@doorbar2012; @egawa2017]. The contrast between productive controls and neoplasia was significant (OR `r fo(stats$m3_or)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m3_p)`). A small number of genuine, non-cell-line skin lesions also harboured unambiguous productive infection, most strikingly an HPV12-productive cSCC and two lesions co-infected with the gamma types HPV96 and HPV182 at near-complete genome coverage and high depth. These cases matter for two reasons. They confirm that bona fide productive cutaneous beta/gamma infection occurs in primary tissue and can be detected from public RNA-seq, which answers the original descriptive question about productive infection. The companion question about non-traditional tissues is not answered here: every one of these libraries is cutaneous, and the residual tier that would have to supply non-cutaneous evidence is defined by missing site metadata rather than by an identified site elsewhere, so this design can bound HPV activity in skin but cannot survey the tissues outside it. They also show that the population-level "trace" conclusion is a statement about the central tendency of cSCC/AK, not a claim that productive cutaneous HPV disease never exists. The picture that emerges aligns with the commensal model of cutaneous HPV [@antonsson2000; @foulongne2012]: a ubiquitous but transcriptionally quiet beta/gamma reservoir in normal skin, overt productive disease confined to warts and EV, and only a residual footprint in carcinoma.

### Contamination is the dominant signal in naïve analyses

Our cell-line finding is both a result and a methodological warning. The roughly five-fold enrichment of HPV positivity in cell-line and engineered libraries, dominated by HPV16/HPV18, mirrors the documented contamination of public sequence archives by HeLa-derived and other integrated-HPV reads [@adey2013; @cantalupo2015; @kazemian2015]. Any survey that pools archived data without flagging non-primary material and without coverage-breadth and depth thresholds will substantially overstate HPV prevalence and mis-attribute mucosal high-risk types to tissues where they have no biological place. The combination we applied, namely explicit cell-line/engineered/in-vitro annotation, study-level curation, dual breadth-and-depth typing thresholds, and depth-normalised burden, is in our view a necessary minimum for credible virus mining of public transcriptomes, and it generalises beyond HPV.

### What the integration marker measures

The E1:E2 ratio was introduced here to separate contaminating cell-line material from genuine infection, and it does that well; but a marker that only ever fires on cultured cells would be indistinguishable from the metadata-based flagging it was meant to check independently. The graded cervical series settles that question in the direction that matters. Across HPV16-positive normal epithelium, high-grade lesion and carcinoma, sequenced under one protocol and labelled by the submitting study, the ratio moves monotonically with grade in primary tissue with no cell line anywhere in the series, and late transcription falls away along the same axis. The marker is therefore reading integration as a biological process rather than culture as a provenance, which is what licenses its use on skin: when it reports the cutaneous reservoir as episomal and quiet, that is a statement about the virus, not an echo of how the libraries were annotated. The series is small, and the normal-epithelium arm in particular rests on few informative libraries, so it establishes the direction of the marker rather than a calibrated scale. It is also worth being explicit about what the cervical data are not doing here. They are not a matched mucosal counterpart to the skin cohort, and the two are not contrasted quantitatively: the comparison that carries weight is within the cervical progression itself, where the confounders that separate any two archived cohorts, depth, protocol, selection and provenance, are held constant by design.

### What a petabase catalogue does and does not measure

The DNA axis used here is a catalogue, and catalogues answer a narrower question than they appear to. The Logan-wide papillomavirus survey identifies contigs by profile-HMM filtering with identification of the conserved L1 B and I domains [@shenpv2026], over an assembly of 27 million archived sequencing libraries [@chikhi2024], so a contig enters the catalogue because it carries a detectable L1. Three consequences follow, and together they bound what any comparison against such a resource can claim. First, presence in the catalogue means L1-detectable presence, and carries no information about the state of the viral genome. Second, the catalogue is assembly-based, and an integrated genome cannot assemble across the virus-host junction, so integrated molecules are systematically under-recovered: conditioning on near-complete contigs returns an intact E2 in 99.3% of cervical carcinoma contigs against 99.9% in skin (@supptbl-e2), which is close to a tautology rather than a biological result, because the completeness criterion has already selected episomal genomes in both. Third, because every contig is anchored on L1 and extends outward from it, the frequency with which an open reading frame is truncated at a contig terminus tracks its distance from that anchor rather than the position of any breakpoint; the ordering E1 > E2 > L1 holds in every body site examined, including healthy vaginal and gut carriage, where integration cannot explain it. Genome state therefore has to be read from reads or from transcription rather than from catalogue membership, which is what the E1:E2 ratio and the virus-host junctions do above. The point generalises beyond papillomaviruses: petabase-scale surveys are now the standard way to establish that a virus is present in a body site, and a presence count from such a survey is not evidence of an active infection.

### Strengths and limitations

The principal strengths of this work are its scale, its uniform end-to-end processing of heterogeneous public data, and its explicit control of the depth and contamination confounders that limit prior reports. Recovering discarded non-human reads turns a vast existing resource toward a question it was never collected to answer [@edgar2022], and reading productivity directly from the early/late transcript programme provides a biologically grounded activity measure rather than mere presence/absence.

Several limitations temper interpretation. First, the unbiased prevalence sweep screened `r comma(stats$n_screened)` libraries, a large but not exhaustive sample of public human skin RNA-seq: of roughly 12,200 candidate runs discovered, the remainder were lost to withdrawn accessions, download failures or quality-control exclusion, and archival sampling is itself non-random, so the absolute healthy-skin positivity rate is best read as an estimate. Second, library selection biases viral recovery: poly-A-selected protocols can deplete viral transcripts, and library types are heterogeneous across studies, so absence of HPV reads is not proof of absence of virus, and our productivity estimates are conservative. Third, tissue and diagnosis labels were derived programmatically from sample metadata and are imperfect, despite curation; residual misclassification adds noise to the tier assignments. Fourth, the high sequence similarity among HPV types permits cross-mapping, which we mitigated with breadth/depth thresholds and multimapping-aware alignment but cannot wholly exclude; the same caveat attaches to distinguishing low-level true infection from residual contaminant signal at the detection floor. Fifth, our data are transcriptomic and cross-sectional: we cannot observe viral DNA persistence, integration state, or the temporal decline in viral activity that the hit-and-run model specifies, and we therefore describe the productive-status phenomenology rather than prove the mechanism. Finally, the L1-based productivity rule, while deliberately stringent, depends on beta/gamma gene annotation quality and treats integrated-line L1 signal cautiously (reported only in the supplement).

### Conclusion

Mining the reads that transcriptomic studies routinely throw away, we find that the cutaneous HPV reservoir of healthy skin is real but transcriptionally quiet, that productive cutaneous HPV infection is the property of warts and EV, and that HPV in cutaneous squamous neoplasia, at population scale and independent of sequencing depth, is a trace, non-productive footprint rather than an active infection. This transcriptomic phenotype is the common ground that both the hit-and-run and the protective-immunity models of beta-HPV in skin cancer must explain. Distinguishing between them will require matched DNA- and RNA-level profiling across the precursor-to-carcinoma transition, single-cell or spatial resolution of where the residual virus resides, and linkage to host antiviral immunity. The public-archive mining framework developed here, with its contamination controls and depth normalisation, provides a scalable foundation for that work.
